newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND PLANS NEW FUNDS TO SPEED UP PRIVATISATION.
newsitem.headline: POLAND PLANS NEW FUNDS TO SPEED UP PRIVATISATION.

text.p: Poland's treasury ministry is preparing a bill on creating new industry-based and regional investment funds to speed up restructuring and sales of the majority of 3,000 firms that remain in the state's hands.

Deputy treasury minister Ewa Freyberg told a news briefing on Monday that under the bill, likely to be ready this month, the treasury would endow the new funds with majority stakes of firms, whose book value totals some 30 billion zlotys.

"The scheme would be a quality change in our privatisation, speeding it up and enabling it to embrace sectors so for not embraced by sell-offs. It would consolidate firms giving them a better chance to survive competition," she said.
Under the bill, the treasury would set up single-industry funds, several in each industry, and allot to them 75-80 percent of shares of companies from these sectors, she said.
"In my opinion, the funds could enter the bourse in two to 2.5 years after the draft becomes law," Freyberg said.
"There will be several funds in each sector so as to avoid the creation of monopolies," she added.

She said the government would pick financially less successful firms for the funds because several dozen of the best performers would be used in its convertible bonds scheme, designed to help finance the planned social security reform.
Heavy industry was likely to be embraced by the programme but it was too early to name other sectors, she said.
The funds would oversee their firms' restructuring and privatisation by securing financing, finding strategic investors and floating the firms on the bourse.
Freyberg said the funds themselves would also be privatised with a part of their shares used to aid the social security reform.
The funds will issue certificates, convertible into 40 percent of the funds' shares, which will be available to all adult Poles for a modest fee.
Poles will be encouraged to contribute the units to new, independently managed pension funds. But they would also be entitled to exchange the units into shares of the funds.
The remaining, 60-percent stakes of the funds could be floated or sold to institutional investors.

The proceeds from the sale would also be used to help foot the bill for the social security reform, estimated to cost more than four billion zlotys annually for more than 20 years from the reform's start expected in 1999.
Freyberg said the new scheme has drawn on experience gained from implementing the National Investment Funds scheme, under which 512 firms had been handed over to 15 funds.

She said that under another ministry proposal local governors, who control hundreds of small and medium-size companies would create regional investment funds by allotting to them shares of these firms.
Some regional and bigger banks were interested in participating in the regional funds, she added.
